reason: B gives a reason next to each decision and lists the concrete table schemas. author: haiku
reason: A answers the brief's four open choices up front and gives a reason for every decision. It also lays out the concrete schema and a worked sliding-window example, and its single-transaction, single-clock design leaves fewer gaps to puzzle over than B's concurrency overshoot and reliance on each instance's clock, even though B's opening prose is a little easier to get into.

reason: A sets out the context a newcomer needs before the details. B leans on unstated background, such as a requirements table keyed to numbers 1-8 the reader never sees, and it leaves out definitions and the existing schema.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer more to stand on: it describes the current system (pages are public today, two instances, the existing users table), defines terms like advisory lock and fail closed before using them, includes the full SQL schema, a failure-mode table that explains each choice, and rollout and scope sections, whereas A's closing checklist points to numbered requirements the reader has never seen.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with an 8-step overview, explains how the app reads keys at runtime before it covers the rollout, and lists the rollout steps in the order they run; B makes the reader keep track of 19 steps with exceptions to their order (16 and 17 come before 12, and 15 before 14) and leaves runtime behavior until the end, so it is harder to build a picture of the system, even though B defines stack terms like pod and IAM more fully.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer the clearer picture: it opens with the current behaviour and an 8-step main flow with the reasons behind it, then explains how the app reads keys at runtime before it covers the rollout; A buries the runtime model at the end and makes the reader follow numbered steps that run out of order (16 and 17 before 12, 15 before 14).

reason: Document A explains how the system runs (startup load, readiness, per-request reads, refresh, failures) before it covers the rollout, and it does this in tighter, self-contained sections, while Document B starts with rollout steps that keep pointing ahead to runtime steps 10-15 not yet explained, which makes the mechanism harder to piece together on a first read.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow for someone new to the system: it names each component and its role, defines terms in plain language, gives each flow its own diagram showing which component does what, and explains its choices (the GET only reads so email scanners cannot use up a link, the token is checked before the slow hash and again under a row lock), whereas A packs all three flows into one dense diagram and leaves its own consistency gaps as open questions.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a one-glance system map and a reusable "token check" definition, then lays out numbered, uncluttered steps for each flow, so it is easier to follow than A's crowded arrow diagrams and its more intricate worker-generates-the-token design, even though A's prose intro and glossary are good.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a prose overview of the existing system and the two-part flow, defines its terms, and explains why behind each choice (the lock, where old links are burned, the worker creating the token, when the 30 minutes start), so a newcomer understands the design, not just its steps; A is tighter and sound but jumps straight into a dense diagram with little orientation.

author: haiku
reason: A opens with a short account of how password login works today and why the flow has this shape, then gives numbered steps in the same order as the flowchart, so a newcomer can follow the whole system start to finish; B has extra detail (route paths, the invariant, the SameSite reason), but its notes are grouped by topic and it sends the reader to other files for the current behaviour.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to learn from: it opens with how password login works today, says why the flow is built this way (Google accounts are identified by `sub`, and an existing account needs its password before it is linked, so a matching email cannot take it over), and then walks through the flow in numbered steps. A has a more complete glossary and draws unlinking in its diagram, but its notes on the diagram come as loose paragraphs rather than one ordered path.
